query: FeNiCrCoCu is considered suitable for thin-film use, and its expense favors applying it as a protective coating on conventional metals rather than using it in bulk. Earlier studies examined room-temperature wear behavior in relation to coating–substrate combinations, composition, and grain size, but largely addressed the alloy itself or a limited thermal regime rather than the overall wear response of a coating across different temperatures. Under the constraints that FeNiCrCoCu remains a thin protective coating and that high-temperature wear is the target application, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its overall wear resistance and why? Specify an intervention relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the observations expected if the hypothesis is correct, state the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, connect the hypothesis to prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: For high-temperature sliding wear, the overall wear resistance of the FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coating is governed by the formation and stability of an adaptive protective oxide layer that forms during a controlled pre-oxidation treatment (or slight Cr enrichment). This oxide layer acts as a barrier, reducing both adhesive and abrasive wear by preventing direct metal-metal contact and mitigating microstructural degradation under high thermal and mechanical stresses.
generation.material_initial_state: As-deposited FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coating with the typical grain structure and phase distribution from deposition on a conventional metal substrate.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled pre-oxidation heat treatment (or a slight Cr enrichment as a compositional tweak) to promote the formation of a continuous, adherent oxide layer prior to high-temperature wear testing.
generation.conditions: High-temperature sliding wear tests conducted between 600°C and 800°C under standardized mechanical loading (e.g., pin-on-disc configuration).
generation.structural_mediator: An adaptive, stable oxide layer (mainly containing oxides of Fe, Cr, Cu, etc.) that forms on the surface during pre-oxidation and remains adherent during wear.
generation.mechanism: The pre-formed oxide layer minimizes direct contact between the coating and the counterface, thereby reducing adhesive and abrasive wear. It also acts to slow down deleterious microstructural changes at high temperature by mitigating the thermal effects that lead to grain coarsening and softening.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline as-deposited coating, the modified coating is expected to show a lower wear rate, evidenced by reduced wear volume and a more continuous, adherent oxide scale observed during SEM/EDS post-test analysis. This layer should persist during sliding and result in a lower coefficient of friction under the high-temperature conditions.
generation.baseline: An as-deposited FeNiCrCoCu coating without intervention (i.e., no controlled pre-oxidation treatment or compositional adjustment).
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable under high-temperature wear conditions (600°C–800°C) with controlled mechanical sliding loads. Its effects are specifically tested on thin-film coatings applied on conventional metal substrates and may not directly translate to bulk materials or different thermal regimes.
generation.uncertainty: While prior studies on similar systems hint at the beneficial role of a controlled oxide layer at elevated temperatures, the long-term stability and self-repair ability of the oxide layer under cyclic loading remain uncertain. Variability in oxide composition and adhesion under different sliding conditions is also not fully established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coatings on conventional metal substrates: one set undergoes a controlled pre-oxidation treatment (or slight Cr enrichment) and the other remains in the as-deposited state. Conduct high-temperature sliding wear tests at temperatures in the 600°C–800°C range under identical mechanical loading (e.g., pin-on-disc tests). Use SEM, EDS, and wear volume measurements to assess the oxide layer quality and wear performance.
measurements: Morphology and continuity of the oxide layer (via SEM/EDS)
Microstructural changes in the coating (grain size, phase transformation)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the intervention does not result in the formation of a more continuous and stable oxide layer, or if the modified coating exhibits no statistically significant reduction in wear rate and coefficient of friction (or even worsened wear behavior with rapid oxide spallation) compared to the as-deposited coating under high-temperature conditions, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.kind: web:3.1. Phase Structure and Morphology of CoCrFeNiMn High-Entropy Alloy Coating
cited_evidence.text: For the room-temperature coating, the high hardness of the coating can resist some abrasive wear and fatigue wear. However, after vacuum heat treatment at 700 °C and 900 °C, due to the decreased hardness of the CS coating, the abrasive wear of the counter-wear ball and quartz sand on the coating surface was intensified, and the crack expansion led to the peeling of the coating.

cited_evidence.kind: web:3.1. Phase Structure and Morphology of CoCrFeNiMn High-Entropy Alloy Coating
cited_evidence.text: In summary, the wear mechanisms of CS and HVOF coatings before and after vacuum heat treatment are adhesive wear, abrasive wear, fatigue wear and oxidation wear. The CS coating is mainly abrasive wear, and the HVOF coating is mainly oxidative wear, adhesive wear and fatigue wear due to the formation of oxides and layered structure during vacuum heat treatment.

The wear rates of the two coatings at room temperature are very close. The wear rate for the CS and HVOF coatings reaches its the lowest point after vacuum heat treatment at 500 °C. The wear rate of the CS-500 °C coating is 0.2152 mm3 m−1 N−1, which is about 4/5 (0.2651 mm3 m−1 N−1) of that of the HVOF-500 °C coating. The CS coating with 500 °C vacuum heat treatment has the best wear resistance due to having the highest microhardness. The wear rates and wear amounts of the two coatings heat-treated at 700 °C and 900 °C decreases due to the decrease in microhardness. The wear mechanisms of the CS and HVOF coatings before and after vacuum heat treatment are adhesive wear, abrasive wear, fatigue wear and oxidation wear.

frame.goal: Explain and improve the overall wear resistance of the coating under high-temperature conditions.

frame.understanding: Hypothesis: The wear resistance of the thin-film FeNiCrCoCu coating at high temperature is governed by the formation and stability of an adaptive protective oxide layer during thermal exposure. This oxide layer, which forms preferentially (especially when optimized by minor compositional tweaks such as an increased Cr content or via a controlled pre-oxidation treatment), mitigates adhesive and abrasive wear by acting as a barrier to direct metal-to-metal contact and slowing down deleterious microstructural transformations. Intervention: Modify the baseline coating by implementing a pre-oxidation heat treatment (or slight compositional adjustment, e.g., slightly enriched Cr) prior to wear testing at high temperatures. Expected observations if the hypothesis is correct include: a more continuous, adherent, and possibly self-repairing oxide scale on the modified coating, reduced wear rates during high-temperature sliding tests compared to the untreated baseline, and observable differences in microstructural degradation. The applicable test conditions are within the 600°C–800°C temperature window under standardized sliding loads. Prior evidence connecting grain boundary characteristics and composition to wear performance (albeit at lower temperatures) supports this proposed mechanism. A result that would falsify this hypothesis would be if the intervention fails to produce a stable oxide layer—i.e., the modified coating shows no improvement in wear resistance, exhibits rapid oxide spallation, or even demonstrates accelerated wear compared to the baseline coating under the same high-temperature conditions.
